clue.text: Biff's one that's odd when alone

blocks.note: to biff someone is to land a blow on them, and there is a four-letter verb for that
these come in pairs, so a single one left in the drawer has no partner

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is all in 'odd': one of a pair left by itself is an odd one, while the surface is offering you 'odd' in the sense of peculiar.
explanation.definitionFit: Biff is a punch and to sock someone is to hit them; the second sense is the garment, which looks wrong alone because they come in pairs.

clue.text: Deletes with a sweep of the pen - or leaves

definitions.text: Deletes with a sweep of the pen

blocks.clueFragment: Deletes with a sweep of the pen
blocks.note: one line drawn through a word cancels it on the page
the sense of setting off somewhere new, as a pioneer does on their own

explanation.walkthrough: The dash does the misdirecting: 'or leaves' looks like more about the pen, when it is a whole second definition and it is about departure.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is drawing a line through writing to cancel it; the other is setting off in a new direction, as in striking out on your own.

clue.text: Summit where you find a pear

blocks.note: a summit is a top-level meeting of leaders, talks rather than a mountain
the long green variety that fills British greengrocers carries this name

explanation.walkthrough: 'Where you find' is only joinery, and no letters are hidden anywhere: the two senses sit side by side, one from diplomacy and one from the fruit bowl.
explanation.definitionFit: A summit is a meeting of heads of state; the other sense is Britain's commonest pear variety, so the fruit defines by example.

clue.text: Dig in pit - bone part fragments - run away

indicators.note: to break a thing into fragments is to leave nothing whole, and letters in pieces are letters free to be laid out in a new order
what has gone away is no longer present, so the letter it names never joins the pile being shuffled

blocks.note: R is the cricket scorer's mark for a run, and this is the letter that goes
eleven letters with that R removed, leaving ten to rearrange

explanation.walkthrough: A pit, a bone and a run make a grim little archaeology scene, and none of it survives: the whole sentence after the first two words is raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: Dig in → BON APPETIT: both are what a host says as food reaches the table, one blunt English and one borrowed straight from French.

clue.text: 'Best'? 'Select'? Everyman is!? Um ...

blocks.note: to select between things is to opt for one
the setter refers to himself as I, so his name plus 'is' contracts to I'm
the hesitation noise, taken down letter for letter

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is somebody groping for the right compliment and trailing off. That trailing off is not decoration: the noise at the end is two of the seven letters.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Best' → OPTIMUM: the optimum is the most favourable point available, so where best ranks things, this names the one that comes top.

clue.text: French city's answer: their refusal, German setter Victor rebuffed

indicators.note: to rebuff is to push back what was offered, so the little pile just built is pushed back and read the other way round

blocks.note: A is the standard short form of answer, as in a quiz's Q and A
French for no, and 'their' points back at the country in the definition
G is the usual single letter for German
the setter is the person writing the clue, and in a clue that person is I
Victor is V in the phonetic alphabet, alongside Charlie and Romeo

explanation.walkthrough: 'German' sits right beside 'refusal' and offers you NEIN. The refusal is French, like the city, and German is doing nothing but its single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: French city → AVIGNON: the walled town on the Rhône that housed the popes in the fourteenth century, still a city in its own right.

clue.text: Stopgap team's assembled: it's stuck in the corner

indicators.note: a thing assembled has been put together out of loose parts, so these letters are built up into an arrangement they did not arrive in

blocks.note: twelve letters, taken exactly as they stand

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stopgap' promises a makeshift arrangement and 'team's assembled' a squad turning up; neither survives into the answer, which is a thing on an envelope.
explanation.definitionFit: it's stuck in the corner → POSTAGE STAMP: the little gummed square you lick and press into the top right of an envelope before posting.

clue.text: Dog story related

indicators.note: a story that is related is one told out loud, so what you write down is a spelling of what the ear receives

blocks.note: a story is a tale, and said aloud that word can just as well be written the other way

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dog story' reads as one phrase and is two: the first word is a verb, and only the second is being sounded out.
explanation.definitionFit: Dog → TAIL: to dog someone is to follow them everywhere, which is exactly what a detective is told to do to a suspect.

clue.text: Lacking shred of compassion, twice cut up ballerina's clothing

indicators.note: to lack something is to be without it, so whatever gets named next never makes it into the letters
this is a down entry, and a piece written up runs from the bottom of the grid towards the top, so its letters arrive in the opposite order

blocks.note: a shred is the smallest scrap of a thing, so this is the letter compassion opens on, and it is the one to lose
CUT climbing a down entry reads T-U-C, and the C just named comes off the end
the same pair written out a second time, one straight after the other

explanation.walkthrough: The surface accuses somebody of heartlessness, and every word of it turns out to be machinery: even 'twice' is an instruction rather than a description.
explanation.definitionFit: ballerina's clothing → TUTU: the stiff layered skirt a ballet dancer performs in, so the definition names her costume rather than any outfit.

clue.text: Research - but seemingly no development - in S African money?

indicators.note: the phrase sets up a familiar pair, then says its second half is not there after all — a letter missing, not a project stalling

blocks.note: the everyday shorthand for a company's research-and-development arm sets two initials either side of the little joining word
the final letter of that shorthand stands for development, and it is the one to drop

explanation.walkthrough: 'Research' looks like a definition and is really an abbreviation written out in full. The dashes sell it as a complaint about a stalled project.
explanation.definitionFit: S African money → RAND: the currency unit of South Africa, named after the Witwatersrand gold reef the country's wealth came out of.

clue.text: Date skin: it's cooked for restrictive regimen

indicators.note: food that has been cooked has been broken down and remade, and a cooked set of letters comes out in a shape it did not go in as

blocks.note: ten letters, taken exactly as they stand

explanation.walkthrough: 'Date skin' offers you dried fruit or a beauty tip, and 'it's cooked' reads as slang for finished. Both are only letters and the instruction to move them.
explanation.definitionFit: restrictive regimen → ATKINS DIET: the low-carbohydrate plan named after Robert Atkins, so it is one particular eating regime rather than dieting in general.

clue.text: Classic song - hit - source of illumination

blocks.note: a song from the old repertoire that every band is expected to know goes by this name
to lamp someone is British slang for hitting them hard

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are decoys from the music business: one is a jazz musician's word, and 'hit' is not a chart-topper at all but a punch.
explanation.definitionFit: source of illumination → STANDARD LAMP: the British name for a floor lamp, a tall light standing on its own stem beside a chair.

clue.text: Taking forever?

blocks.note: not the time a job takes: this is taking in the sense of taking things that are not yours
not a long wait either, but an urge that never lets up, however little is worth having

explanation.walkthrough: There is nothing to take apart here, only one phrase read twice: the impatient grumble about a slow queue turns into a clinical condition.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking forever? → KLEPTOMANIA: a compulsion to steal that never lets up, so a grumble about slowness doubles as endless helpless thieving.

clue.text: Sir, you'll go off in magnificent style

indicators.note: milk that has gone off has turned and is no longer what it was, and letters that turn will not stay in the order they were handed over

blocks.note: ten letters, apostrophe ignored, taken as they stand

explanation.walkthrough: 'Go off' looks like a single instruction, which costs you two letters: 'go' is material, and only the little word after it is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: in magnificent style → GLORIOUSLY: to do a thing gloriously is to do it with splendour and to acclaim, which is the adverb the phrase asks for.

clue.text: With no hint of nervousness, taunt leader that's corrupt, corrupt

indicators.note: with no X means X is absent, so the letter named straight afterwards never joins the mix
something corrupt has been tampered with and no longer stands as it was, so these letters are out of their proper order

blocks.note: a hint of a word is the letter it opens on, and this is the one taken out
eleven letters with that N gone, leaving ten to rearrange

explanation.walkthrough: The setter writes the same word twice and gives it two jobs: the first tells you to disturb the letters, the second says what they add up to.
explanation.definitionFit: corrupt → ADULTERATE: to adulterate is to spoil something pure by mixing a cheaper substance in, the sense of corrupt that applies to goods.

clue.text: Total including seabird's bone

indicators.note: to include a thing is to have it inside you rather than beside you, so one word opens up and the other takes the gap

blocks.note: the total of a column of figures is its sum
a tern is the small fork-tailed sea bird, and it is the crossword's default one

explanation.walkthrough: The possessive in 'seabird's' is doing link duty rather than belonging to anyone: the bird is the wordplay and the word after it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: bone → STERNUM: the flat breastbone running down the front of the ribcage, so the clue names one particular bone by its anatomical word.

clue.text: About 50 wanted to be annoyed

indicators.note: to put something about a thing is to wrap round it, so one piece opens and takes the other into the middle of itself

blocks.note: wanted in the past tense, six letters
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.walkthrough: 'About' is most often C for circa in a cryptic, and here it is the wrapping instruction instead. The tense of 'wanted' is what makes the letters fit.
explanation.definitionFit: annoyed → NEEDLED: to needle someone is to prod them with small jabs until they are irritated, so the past participle matches the mood.

clue.text: Relative mostly visible with snake - let go!

indicators.note: what is mostly visible is not entirely visible, so the word keeps its last letter out of sight

blocks.note: a relative may be an uncle, and here the final E stays out of view
the asp is the small venomous snake of Egypt, and three letters make it a crossword regular

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a warning shouted at somebody gripping a snake. That shout is the definition, and everything in front of it is construction.
explanation.definitionFit: let go → UNCLASP: to unclasp is to open the grip of fingers or of a fastening, so whatever was being held is released.

clue.text: Unwisely, I had most of pâté stir-fry

indicators.note: to act unwisely is to act without sense or order, and letters handled without order come out in a new arrangement
most of a word is all but a little of it, so the word hands over everything except its final letter

blocks.note: four letters exactly as written
the French spread, with its final letter left off

explanation.walkthrough: 'Unwisely, I had...' sets up a confession about a bad meal, and the pâté is the giveaway: it is a French delicacy on the surface and three letters underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: stir-fry → PAD THAI: the Thai dish of rice noodles tossed fast in a hot wok, so it is one example of the form rather than the form.

clue.text: Idolater almost concealing cunning manner of thinking

definitions.note: The clue defines the whole phrase 'lateral thinking'; the answer is only its first word, the adjective that heads it.

indicators.note: to conceal a thing is to keep it out of sight inside something else, so the letters wanted are running unbroken through the words in front

blocks.note: seven letters in a single unbroken run across these two words, starting in the middle of the first

explanation.walkthrough: 'Idolater almost' looks like an instruction to trim a word, which is the trap: it is the hiding place, and the join falls inside a word rather than at the space.
explanation.definitionFit: cunning manner of thinking → LATERAL: lateral thinking comes at a problem from the side instead of head on, which is where its cleverness lies.

clue.text: Act dishonestly, getting stuffing for duvet - then do this?

definitions.note: The definition is a pointer rather than a synonym: it tells you to perform the action the clue's own two pieces have just spelled out.

blocks.note: to act dishonestly in speech is to tell an untruth
the soft under-feathers a quilt is filled with

explanation.walkthrough: The definition arrives last and points backwards: having built the phrase, the clue simply tells you to go and do it. Both pieces are bedroom words already.
explanation.definitionFit: then do this → LIE DOWN: after a duvet has been stuffed you stretch out on the bed, so the phrase names the very action its pieces spell.

clue.text: Comic actor Rod: you led me astray

indicators.note: something led astray has been taken off its proper path, and letters off their path are letters out of order

blocks.note: eleven letters, taken as they stand

explanation.walkthrough: The clue dangles a first name at you, so 'Rod' reads as the man being named. It is the first three letters of the shuffle instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Comic actor → DUDLEY MOORE: the British comedian and pianist of Beyond the Fringe and Arthur, so the definition names his trade exactly.

clue.text: Primarily cinnamony, hot Asian infusion?

indicators.note: what comes primarily comes before everything else, so each word gives up only the character it opens with

blocks.note: the opening letter of each of the four words, read in the order they stand

explanation.walkthrough: An all-in-one: the sentence is the recipe and the description at once, and the question mark admits this is not the only spiced hot drink going.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue describes the drink: chai is a spiced Indian tea, cinnamon among its spices, drunk hot as an infusion of leaves.

clue.text: Huge eerie deathcap fungi: panic, ultimately

indicators.note: what happens ultimately happens at the very end, so each word in the run gives up the letter it finishes on and nothing else

blocks.note: the closing letter of each of these four words, read in the order they stand

explanation.walkthrough: The mushroom hunt is a decoy: deathcaps and panic build a poisoning scene, and every word in it is there only for the letter it ends on.
explanation.definitionFit: Huge → EPIC: an epic effort is one on a vast scale, the adjective having drifted from the long heroic poem to anything outsized.

clue.text: No help - that's scuppered contest

indicators.note: a scuppered boat has been holed and sunk, so what stood in good order ends up in a heap

blocks.note: ten letters, taken as they stand

explanation.walkthrough: The Greek hepta is seven and athlon a contest, so the answer says 'seven contests' on its own, which is why one word can define it.
explanation.definitionFit: contest → HEPTATHLON: the seven-event athletics competition decided over two days, so it is one particular contest rather than contests in general.

clue.text: Fantasias describing most of humanity

indicators.note: to describe a circle is to draw a line right round it, so the word that describes has these letters enclosed within it

blocks.note: one word holds four consecutive letters, starting at its fifth

explanation.walkthrough: 'Most of' is the standard signal for chopping a letter off a word, and here it belongs to the definition instead — a plain statement of population.
explanation.definitionFit: most of humanity → ASIA: about six in ten people alive are Asian, so the continent genuinely holds the majority of the human race.

clue.text: Starts off nine optics

indicators.note: something that has gone off has turned and no longer holds its shape, so these letters will not stay as they were given

blocks.note: ten letters, taken as they stand

explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts off' looks like one phrase and splits down the middle: the noun in front is the definition, and the little word after it is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Starts → INCEPTIONS: an inception is the moment a thing begins, so the plural names beginnings in a formal word where 'starts' is the plain one.

clue.text: Slice of memory: snack picked up

indicators.note: what is picked up is caught by the ear, so the wordplay hands you a sound and leaves the spelling to you

blocks.note: a small snack is a bite, and said aloud that word can be written another way

explanation.walkthrough: 'Slice of memory' looks like an instruction to cut letters out of the word 'memory'. It is the definition, and the whole mechanism is in the ear.
explanation.definitionFit: Slice of memory → BYTE: eight bits, the unit computer storage is counted in, so a portion of memory is measured in these.
